questions.why: The external path depends on the listener, routing, and security rules together; checking only the backend security group may miss the public load-balancer path.

questions.q: A user gets a valid MFA push after entering a password into a fake page. What is the best immediate containment?
choices: Deny the push and reset the password but leave active sessions
Change the password from a trusted bookmark; review sessions later
Deny the push and report it, then watch for another attempt
Deny, report, reset via a trusted path, and review sessions
questions.why: The push suggests the password was captured, so deny it, report the event, reset through a trusted route, and review active sessions; a password change alone can leave sessions valid.

questions.q: An organization has backups but never tests restoration. Which risk remains highest during ransomware recovery?
choices: The backup may be unusable or miss required systems
The backup is too old but its contents are otherwise usable
The backup was encrypted but the key may be unavailable
The backup may omit an application dependency at restore
questions.why: A restore test checks integrity and dependencies needed for recovery; having backup files alone does not prove restorability.

questions.q: A server accepts client certificates but grants every certificate the same administrator role. What control is missing?
choices: Network segmentation that limits access to the service
Authorization tied to identity and least privilege
Shorter certificate validity to reduce exposure time
Stronger TLS cipher suites for the client connections
questions.why: Certificates authenticate clients but do not assign appropriate permissions; TLS encryption alone cannot limit actions.

questions.q: A team has a signed software package from an unfamiliar key. What should they verify before installing?
choices: A checksum that matches the same download page
A second mirror serving the same unknown signature
Verify publisher-key identity and package integrity
A signature from any key found in the archive
questions.why: A signature matters only when its key belongs to the expected publisher; a matching checksum from the same untrusted page does not establish that identity.

questions.q: A vendor needs temporary access to one system. Which approach best limits residual risk?
choices: A shared admin account with a fixed removal date
A named account with scoped access but no expiry
A temporary VPN account with broad internal reach
Use named, scoped access with expiry and audit logs
questions.why: Named, scoped, expiring access can be audited and removed; a shared permanent password cannot be attributed or bounded.

questions.q: A switch learns the same MAC on two ports every few seconds. What is the best first hypothesis and check?
choices: Check topology and port events for a loop or MAC move
A DHCP address conflict; compare leases for both ports
A routing loop; inspect only the hosts default routes
A DNS split view; compare the resolver answers
questions.why: Frequent MAC moves can arise from a loop or mobility, so inspect topology and port events; a DHCP lease conflict does not explain layer-2 MAC learning.

questions.q: A client has address 192.0.2.70/26 and gateway 192.0.2.1. Why can it not reach the gateway directly?
choices: They share the 192.0.2 prefix, so direct ARP should work
The gateway is outside the client's /26 subnet
The gateway needs a DNS record before the host can ARP
The client can broadcast through the router to reach it
questions.why: 192.0.2.70/26 belongs to .64–.127 while .1 is in .0–.63; direct gateway ARP will not work across those subnets.

questions.q: A trunk carries VLAN 20 but a host on VLAN 20 reaches only local peers, not its gateway. What should be checked first?
choices: The host default route and configured gateway address
DNS resolution for a host beyond the local VLAN
VLAN 20 across the trunk and its gateway interface
The gateway address and route on a different VLAN
questions.why: Local switching can work when the routed gateway path is broken; a correct host default route alone does not prove VLAN 20 reaches its gateway.

questions.q: A capture shows TCP retransmissions after a switch port reports CRC errors. What is the best first physical check?
choices: Inspect NIC driver version before checking the physical link
Increase TCP receive buffers to accommodate packet loss
Adjust application retries before examining CRC errors
Inspect cable and switch-port health on the affected link
questions.why: CRC errors point to link corruption that can cause retransmissions; a driver update before checking cable and port health skips the direct evidence.

questions.q: Two DHCP servers answer one client's request with different gateways. What symptom is most likely?
choices: Routing varies with the gateway in the accepted offer
Intermittent name resolution when DNS TTL values differ
Duplicate IP addresses for clients receiving either offer
No address assignment because two offers cancel each other
questions.why: Different accepted offers can give different default routes, causing inconsistent connectivity; DHCP can still assign an address.

questions.q: A laptop is slow only while charging; battery mode is normal. What should be compared first?
choices: Compare battery health and capacity while in both modes
Compare power settings, adapter detection, and heat
Benchmark storage in both power modes to isolate slowdown
Update the display driver and compare graphics performance
questions.why: Charging can change performance and heat policy, so compare power and thermal evidence; replacing the battery before checking those differences is premature.

questions.q: A desktop powers on with fans but no display after RAM replacement. What is the narrowest first check?
choices: Check firmware settings for the new memory profile
Test the monitor cable with another working computer
Reseat compatible RAM; test one module in the correct slot
Boot external media to check whether the OS is damaged
questions.why: A memory seating or compatibility issue can prevent POST before video; OS and disk checks come later.

questions.q: A user can print a test page locally but not from one application. What should support isolate next?
choices: Reinstall the driver on the affected workstation
Reset the queue and print a second local test page
Check printer IP settings and compare another app
Check that application’s print settings and document path
questions.why: A local test page proves the basic printer path, so focus on the affected app; resetting the shared print queue may disrupt others without addressing its settings.

questions.q: A drive reports rising reallocated sectors and the user has no recent backup. What is the best order?
choices: Back up readable data, then replace and diagnose the drive
Run a long diagnostic before copying data off the drive
Move files to another partition on the same drive first
Defragment the drive before making a backup copy
questions.why: Preserving data comes first when failure signs appear; a stress test may worsen a marginal drive before backup.

questions.q: Two users share a Windows PC; one user's profile cannot open an app, but the other can. What is the best initial isolation?
choices: Repair the app install for all users before checking profiles
Compare user settings and permissions before reinstalling
Compare system firewall rules with another working PC
Create a new profile and migrate files before comparison
questions.why: A per-user difference points to profile or permission state; a system-wide reinstall is premature.

steps.q: 7:02 AM. Five calls to the help desk: files on the shared drive now end in .lckd and a note demands Bitcoin. What do you do first?
choices: Isolate the affected machines from the network
Pay the ransom before it goes up
Reboot every server to stop it
Email the whole campus the technical details
steps.why: Containment comes first: cut infected machines off (pull the network or quarantine them with EDR) so encryption cannot spread. Rebooting can destroy evidence in memory.

steps.q: 7:20 AM. EDR shows the encryption started on one staff laptop, FIN-LT-14. What do you preserve before rebuilding it?
choices: A memory image, a disk image, and the EDR and firewall logs
Nothing: rebuild it right away
Only a photo of the ransom note
The user's browser bookmarks
steps.why: Evidence shows how the attacker got in and what else they touched. Without it you may rebuild the same hole.

steps.q: 8:05 AM. The nightly backup server sat on the same domain and is encrypted too. What saves you?
choices: The offline, immutable weekly backup, after a test restore
The attacker's decryptor
Shadow copies on the infected server
Re-running last night's backup job
steps.why: Attackers hunt for backups first. Offline or immutable copies, tested regularly, are what make recovery possible without paying.

steps.q: 9:30 AM. Leadership asks whether to pay. What is the best guidance?
choices: It is a leadership decision with legal, insurers and law enforcement (FBI / IC3); paying does not guarantee recovery
Always pay: it is the fastest option
Keep leadership out of it
Let the attackers talk to students directly
steps.why: Payment is a business and legal decision, not the SOC's alone, and it can be restricted. Report to law enforcement either way.

steps.q: 11:00 AM. Logs show data was copied to an unknown cloud storage site before the encryption started. What does that change?
choices: It may be a data breach: bring in legal and privacy for notification duties (for example FERPA and state law)
Nothing: the encryption was the only problem
Delete those logs to limit liability
Only block the ransom note's email address
steps.why: Modern ransomware steals data first, then encrypts. Stolen student records can trigger legal notification requirements.

steps.q: One week later. Root cause: the attacker signed in to the VPN with a staff password and no MFA. Best lesson-learned action?
choices: Require MFA on the VPN and all remote access, and rehearse the incident plan
Ban laptops for staff
Move the VPN to a different port
Name the staff member publicly
steps.why: Stolen passwords without MFA are one of the most common ways in. Fix the control, then practice the plan, without blaming people.

steps.q: Payroll gets an email from the 'CFO' asking to change her direct deposit before Friday. It comes from cfo-isu-edu.com. What first?
choices: Verify by calling the CFO on a number you already know; change nothing yet
Make the change: it is the CFO
Reply to the email to ask if it is real
Forward it to the whole finance team
steps.why: Payment changes must be confirmed through a separate, known channel. Replying only reaches the attacker.

steps.q: Three more staff report the same lure. Two of them clicked a link to a 'Microsoft 365' sign-in page. What next?
choices: Reset their passwords, sign them out everywhere, and check their MFA and sign-in logs
Wait to see if anything happens
Just delete the emails
Ask them to change passwords next month
steps.why: Assume the credentials were captured. Revoking sessions matters because attackers can keep a stolen session even after a password change.

steps.q: Sign-in logs show one of those accounts signed in from overseas minutes after the click, and a new inbox rule forwards mail containing 'invoice' to an outside address. What do you do?
choices: Remove the rule, revoke sessions, and review what the attacker read and sent
Leave the rule so you can watch them
Only change the user's display name
Delete the user's whole mailbox
steps.why: Forwarding rules are classic business email compromise persistence. Remove them, then find out what was exposed or sent in the user's name.

steps.q: How do you stop other people from falling for the same email?
choices: Search for and remove it from every mailbox, and block the sender domain and link
Email the attacker asking them to stop
Turn off email for the whole campus
Do nothing: people should know better
steps.why: Email platforms can find and purge a message from all mailboxes. Block the indicators so new copies bounce.

steps.q: Which control would have stopped the stolen password from working at all?
choices: Phishing-resistant MFA, like passkeys or security keys
Making passwords expire more often
Antivirus on every laptop
A VPN for email
steps.why: Passkeys and security keys are tied to the real site, so a fake sign-in page cannot capture anything reusable.

steps.q: What is the best message to staff afterward?
choices: Thank the people who reported it, show the real example, and remind everyone to verify payment changes by phone
Shame the people who clicked
Ban all links in email
Say it was nothing
steps.why: Fast reporting is what limited the damage. Reward it, and keep the lesson concrete.

steps.q: GitHub alerts you that a student's class project repo contains an AWS access key for the department's account. What first?
choices: Deactivate and rotate the key right away
Ask the student to delete the file
Make the repo private and wait
Ignore it: the repo is only a day old
steps.why: Bots scan GitHub for keys within minutes. Deleting the file does not help, because the key stays in git history. Kill the key first.

steps.q: CloudTrail shows the key was used 40 minutes ago to call RunInstances in three regions you never use. What are the attackers most likely doing?
choices: Running cryptomining on expensive instances
Backing up your data
Testing your website
Nothing important
steps.why: Leaked cloud keys are most often used for cryptomining, which can cost thousands of dollars in hours.

choices: Everything the key did: new users, keys, roles, instances and regions
Only the region you normally use
The student's grades
Your DNS records
steps.why: Attackers create persistence (new users, keys or roles) so they keep access after you revoke the first key. Check every region.

steps.q: You find a new IAM user named 'support-admin' that the key created. What do you do?
choices: Record the evidence, then delete it and its keys, and keep hunting for more
Rename it to something safer
Leave it for now
Turn on MFA for it
steps.why: It is the attacker's backdoor. Preserve the details for the report, remove it, and look for other changes.

steps.q: The bill already shows $3,000. Who do you contact?
choices: AWS support, and your leadership and finance office
The student who leaked it, to pay
Nobody: it is already spent
GitHub support
steps.why: Cloud providers have a process for charges caused by compromise. Leadership needs to know about the cost and the incident.

steps.q: How do you stop this from happening again?
choices: Short-lived role credentials, secret scanning before commits, and least-privilege keys
Forbid students from writing code
Make keys longer
Share keys over email instead
steps.why: Short-lived credentials leave nothing useful to leak, and secret scanning catches mistakes before they are pushed.
